title: Linux Examples 1: AT&T Syntax, Calls, Locals, Parameters (part 1 of 2)

questions.q: In AT&T syntax, what does `mov %rsp,%rbp` do?
choices: Copies the value of rbp into rsp
Copies the value of rsp into rbp
Copies the 8 bytes stored at the address in rsp into rbp
Swaps the values of rsp and rbp
questions.explain: AT&T operands go source -> destination (left to right), so rsp is the source and rbp is the destination. Intel syntax writes the same instruction as `mov rbp, rsp`. There are no parentheses, so no memory is accessed.

questions.q: Which Intel-syntax instruction is equivalent to the AT&T instruction `add $0x14,%rsp`?
choices: add 0x14, rsp
add rsp, 0x14
add rsp, [0x14]
add qword ptr [rsp], 0x14
questions.explain: $ marks an immediate and % marks a register. AT&T puts the destination last and Intel puts it first. Both mean rsp = rsp + 0x14.

questions.q: Which of these are features of AT&T syntax, as opposed to Intel syntax?
choices: Registers are written with a % prefix
Immediate values are written with a $ prefix
The destination operand is written last
Memory operand sizes are given with keywords like DWORD PTR
Memory operands are written inside square brackets
Operand size can be shown by a suffix on the mnemonic, as in movl or movq
questions.explain: AT&T uses %reg and $imm, reads source(s) -> destination, and puts size in the mnemonic suffix (b/w/l/q). The DWORD PTR / QWORD PTR keywords and [square brackets] are Intel syntax. AT&T writes memory as disp(base,index,scale).

questions.q: In the AT&T instruction `mov $0x0,%esi`, the operand `$0x0` refers to the memory at address 0.
questions.explain: $ marks an immediate (constant) value. The instruction just puts 0 into esi. In Intel syntax it is `mov esi,0x0`.

questions.q: The AT&T assembly syntax used by GNU tools comes from which earlier assembly syntax?
choices: The syntax in Intel's original 8086 manuals
The PDP-11 assembly syntax that early UNIX was written in
Microsoft's MASM syntax
A syntax GNU designed from scratch for x86-64
questions.explain: Bell Labs went from Multics on mainframes to UNIX in PDP-11 assembly, then rewrote UNIX in C. When UNIX was ported to the 8086, its assembly syntax was adapted from the PDP-11's, and GNU tools inherited that style.

questions.q: Which AT&T instruction is equivalent to the Intel instruction `mov edx,0xa`?
choices: mov %edx,$0xa
mov $0xa,%edx
mov 0xa,%edx
mov %edx,0xa
questions.explain: The source comes first and the destination last, and the immediate gets a $. Without the $, `0xa` would be a memory operand (the contents of address 0xa).

questions.q: How many bytes does an AT&T `movl` instruction move?
questions.explain: l = 'long', which Intel calls a dword: 4 bytes. The suffixes are b = 1 byte, w = 2, l = 4, q = 8.

questions.q: Which AT&T mnemonic suffix marks an operation on a 2-byte value?
choices: b
w
l
q
questions.explain: w = word (2 bytes). b = byte (1), l = long/dword (4), q = quad word/qword (8).

questions.q: The disassembler prints `movl $0xff,0x1010(%rsp)` with a size suffix, but `mov $0xa,%edx` without one. Why?
choices: A suffix is added only when the instruction moves an immediate
In the first instruction, neither the immediate nor the memory operand shows the size, so the suffix is needed. In the second, the register %edx already sets the size to 32 bits
movl is a different, faster instruction than mov
The suffix shows that the destination is on the stack
questions.explain: Per the GNU assembler docs, the size comes from the mnemonic's last character only when there is no other way to disambiguate the instruction. A register operand implies its own size, but an immediate stored to memory does not. Intel writes the first instruction as `mov DWORD PTR [rsp+0x1010],0xff`.

questions.q: What is the Intel-syntax equivalent of `orq $0x0,(%rsp)`?
choices: or rsp, 0x0
or QWORD PTR [rsp],0x0
or DWORD PTR [rsp],0x0
or 0x0, QWORD PTR [rsp]
questions.explain: q = 8 bytes = QWORD PTR. `(%rsp)` means the memory at the address in rsp, which Intel writes as [rsp]. The destination moves to the front.

questions.q: The AT&T instruction `movslq %eax,%rdx` corresponds to which Intel instruction?
choices: movsx eax, rdx
movsxd rdx, eax
movzx rdx, eax
mov rdx, qword ptr [eax]
questions.explain: movs + l + q = move with sign extension, from long (32-bit) to quad (64-bit). Intel calls the dword-to-qword form movsxd and puts the destination first.

questions.q: AT&T syntax renames Intel's `cwde` to `cwtl`. What does `cwtl` stand for?
choices: Clear word, test long
Convert (sign-extend) word to long
Compare word to long
Copy word, truncate long
questions.explain: c-w-t-l = convert word to long. It sign-extends the 16-bit ax into the 32-bit eax, which is what Intel's cwde does. It was renamed to follow the b/w/l/q size naming convention.

questions.q: AT&T mnemonics only ever add a size suffix to the Intel name, so you can always find a mnemonic like `movsbw` by searching the Intel manual for that exact name.
questions.explain: Some mnemonics are renamed, not just given a suffix. movsx becomes movsbw/movswl, movsxd becomes movslq, cwde becomes cwtl, and movabs exists only in GNU's syntax. To look one up, you have to map it back to the Intel name or check the GNU assembler (gas) docs.

questions.q: Intel writes a memory operand as `[base + index*scale + disp]`. How does AT&T write it?
choices: disp(base, index, scale)
(disp, base, index, scale)
base(index, scale, disp)
[base, index, scale] + disp
questions.explain: AT&T moves the displacement outside the parentheses and lists base, index, scale inside. The address operations aren't written out: you have to remember that it means base + index*scale + disp.

questions.q: Which Intel instruction matches the AT&T instruction `callq *-0xe8(%rbx,%rsi,4)`?
choices: call qword ptr [rbx+rsi*4-0xe8]
call qword ptr [rbx*4+rsi-0xe8]
call qword ptr [(rbx+rsi)*4-0xe8]
call rbx+rsi+4-0xe8
questions.explain: disp(base,index,scale) = base + index*scale + disp. Here base = rbx, index = rsi, scale = 4 and disp = -0xe8. The * marks an indirect call through the 8-byte pointer stored at that address.

questions.q: With rbx = 0x1000 and rcx = 3, what address does the AT&T memory operand `-0x8(%rbx,%rcx,8)` refer to? Answer in hex, like 0x1234.
Which AT&T instruction is equivalent to Intel `mov rax, qword ptr [rbp+0x8]`?
choices: movq %rax, 0x8(%rbp)
movq 0x8(%rbp), %rax
movq $0x8(%rbp), %rax
movq (%rbp,0x8), %rax
questions.explain: The memory source [rbp+0x8] becomes 0x8(%rbp) and comes first, and the destination %rax comes last. The q suffix replaces 'qword ptr'. A displacement takes no $, because it isn't an immediate.

questions.q: Which Intel instruction is equivalent to the AT&T instruction `lea 0x1010(%rsp),%rsi`?
choices: lea rsp, [rsi+0x1010]
lea rsi, [rsp+0x1010]
mov rsi, qword ptr [rsp+0x1010]
lea rsi, [rsp*0x1010]
questions.explain: The displacement outside the parentheses becomes +disp inside the brackets, and the destination moves to the front. lea puts the computed address rsp+0x1010 into rsi without reading memory, so it's not the same as the mov.

questions.q: What does the AT&T instruction `mov 0x8(%rsi),%rdi` do?
choices: Puts the value rsi+8 into rdi
Loads the value stored in memory at address rsi+8 into rdi
Stores rdi to memory at address rsi+8
Puts the constant 8 into rdi
questions.explain: disp(base) without a $ is a memory operand, and the source comes first, so this reads memory at rsi+0x8 into rdi. Intel disassembly of the same bytes shows `mov rdi,QWORD PTR [rsi+0x8]`. The AT&T form has no suffix, so it doesn't spell out the size the way QWORD PTR does.

questions.q: What is `endbr64`, the instruction gcc puts at the start of each function in these examples?
choices: A stack-protector check that gcc adds
Part of Intel's Control-flow Enforcement Technology (CET). On processors without CET it acts as a NOP
An instruction that clears branch prediction state at the end of the previous function
A breakpoint that gdb inserts at each function entry
questions.explain: Intel's CET documentation says ENDBR32/ENDBR64 have the same effect as a NOP on Intel 64 processors that don't support CET. The compiler emits it so the code gets the extra protection on systems that have it. On other systems it does nothing.

questions.q: On a processor that does not support CET, executing `endbr64` changes no registers or memory: it behaves like a NOP.
questions.explain: Without CET support, ENDBR64 has the same effect as a NOP, so you can skip over it when reading these listings.

questions.q: In gdb, what is the difference between `ni` and `si` when the current instruction is a `call`?
choices: ni steps over the call to the next instruction in the current function, and si steps into the called function
ni steps into the call, and si steps over it
Both step into the call, but si also prints the source line
ni runs to the end of the current function, and si runs one source line
questions.explain: ni = next instruction (step over calls). si = step instruction (follows the call into the callee). To watch func's prologue, use si at `callq func`.

questions.q: Even the one-line `func` in CallAFunction1 gets a `push %rbp` / `mov %rsp,%rbp` prologue from gcc. Why?
choices: Linux requires a frame pointer in every function
Without an -O flag, gcc compiles with optimization disabled, so it builds a full stack frame even for trivial functions
endbr64 can only follow a frame-pointer prologue
func has local variables that must be addressed through rbp
questions.explain: gcc's default is no optimization, so it creates a standard rbp-based stack frame even when the function only puts a constant in eax and returns.

questions.q: In CallAFunction1, func does `mov $0xbeef,%eax` and returns. Then main does `mov $0xf00d,%eax` before its own epilogue. What value does main return? Answer in hex.
questions.explain: eax holds the return value. main ignores func's 0xbeef and overwrites eax with 0xf00d, so main always returns 0xf00d.

questions.q: func's epilogue is `pop %rbp` followed by `retq`. What does `retq` do?
choices: Pops the value on top of the stack into rip, which returns to the instruction after the call
Copies rbp into rsp and jumps to main
Pops the value on top of the stack into rax as the return value
Jumps to the address held in rbp
questions.explain: After `pop %rbp` restores the caller's frame pointer, the top of the stack holds the return address that `call` pushed. ret pops it into rip.

questions.q: The examples are compiled with gcc's `-fno-stack-protector` option. What does it do?
choices: It turns off gcc's stack-protection (canary) checking code, which keeps the generated assembly simpler
It disables the System V red zone
It stops gcc from emitting endbr64
It makes the stack executable
questions.explain: It removes the extra stack-protector instructions, so the listings show only the code that implements the C source. endbr64 still appears, because it is CET-related, not part of the stack protector.

questions.q: In SingleLocalVariable, `func` runs `movl $0x5ca1ab1e,-0x4(%rbp)`. Where is the local variable i stored?
choices: In the 4 bytes starting at rbp+4
In the 4 bytes starting at rbp-4
In register eax
In the 8 bytes starting at rbp-8
questions.explain: -0x4(%rbp) is the memory at rbp-4. The l suffix makes it a 4-byte store, the size of an int. The next instruction, `mov -0x4(%rbp),%eax`, reads i back into eax to return it.

questions.q: In func, rbp = rsp = 0x7fffffffdf50. At what address is i = 0x5ca1ab1e stored? Answer in hex.
questions.explain: rbp - 4 = 0x7fffffffdf50 - 4 = 0x7fffffffdf4c.

questions.q: In func's stack frame, the saved return address is 0x55555555514f. Which instruction is at that address?
choices: The first instruction of func
The `pop %rbp` in main, right after `callq func`
The `callq func` instruction itself
main's endbr64
questions.explain: call pushes the address of the next instruction. callq is at 0x55555555514a and is 5 bytes long, so the return address is 0x55555555514f, main's `pop %rbp`.

questions.q: main's frame has its saved rbp at 0x7fffffffdf60, and main then sets rbp = rsp. What value does func's `push %rbp` store at 0x7fffffffdf50?
choices: 0x7fffffffdf60, main's frame pointer
0x0, the rbp value from before main ran
0x55555555514f, the return address
0x5ca1ab1e
questions.explain: After main's `mov %rsp,%rbp`, rbp = 0x7fffffffdf60. func pushes that value, and func's `pop %rbp` restores it before returning. The 0x0 is the older rbp that main saved at 0x7fffffffdf60.

questions.q: How many bytes is the red zone in the System V x86-64 ABI?
questions.explain: The ABI reserves the 128-byte area beyond (below) the address in rsp.

questions.q: Which statements about the red zone are true?
choices: It is the area just beyond (below) the address in rsp
Signal and interrupt handlers must not modify it
Leaf functions may use it for their whole stack frame instead of adjusting rsp in the prologue and epilogue
Data stored there is preserved across calls the function makes
It lies above the return address, next to the stack arguments
questions.explain: The ABI says the 128 bytes beyond rsp are reserved and will not be modified by signal or interrupt handlers, so a function may keep temporary data there that is not needed across function calls. Stack arguments are at 16(%rbp) and above, which is above the return address, not in the red zone.

questions.q: In func, rsp and rbp both point at the saved rbp, yet func writes i to rbp-4, below the top of the stack. Why is that safe?
choices: func is a leaf function (it calls nothing), so it can use the red zone below rsp without subtracting from rsp
Writing below rsp is always safe on x86-64
gcc subtracts from rsp in an instruction the debugger hides
rbp-4 belongs to main's frame, which func may reuse
questions.explain: Normally the prologue would subtract from rsp to allocate locals. Because the ABI promises that signal/interrupt handlers won't clobber the 128 bytes below rsp, a leaf function can skip the sub/add and keep its locals there.

questions.q: If func called another function, data func had left in the red zone could be overwritten by that call.
questions.explain: A call pushes the return address at rsp-8, and the callee builds its frame below that, right where the red zone was. That is why the ABI limits the red zone to temporary data not needed across function calls, and why leaf functions are the ones that use it for their whole frame.

questions.q: In the System V 'stack frame with base pointer' layout, what is at 8(%rbp)?
choices: The previous rbp value
The return address
The first memory argument (eightbyte 0)
The first local variable
questions.explain: 0(%rbp) = previous rbp, 8(%rbp) = return address, 16(%rbp) and up = memory arguments (eightbyte 0, 1, ...). Locals sit at negative offsets from rbp.

questions.q: ArrayLocalVariable's disassembly contains `movabs <64-bit constant>,%rax`. What is movabs?
choices: An instruction that moves the absolute value of its operand
The GNU assembler's AT&T name for mov when it uses a 64-bit immediate or 64-bit displacement. It is a plain mov that loads the constant into rax
A mov that uses an absolute address instead of an rbp-relative one
A privileged mov that only the kernel can run
questions.explain: Per the gas docs, in 64-bit code `movabs` can be used to encode the mov instruction with a 64-bit displacement or immediate operand. The Intel manual has no instruction called movabs, so searching it will fail. That is a reason to check the GNU assembler docs when a mnemonic looks unfamiliar.

questions.q: What does `movswl -0x2(%rbp),%eax` do?
choices: Moves the 32-bit value at rbp-2 into eax, swapping its bytes
Sign-extends the 16-bit value at rbp-2 to 32 bits and puts it in eax
Zero-extends the 16-bit value at rbp-2 to 32 bits and puts it in eax
Moves eax to rbp-2 as a 16-bit value
questions.explain: movs = move with sign extension, w = from word (16 bits), l = to long (32 bits). Intel calls this movsx eax, word ptr [rbp-0x2].

questions.q: The short `a = 0xbabe` is sign-extended to 32 bits by `movswl`. What value ends up in eax? Answer in hex.
questions.explain: 0xbabe's top bit is 1 (0xb = 1011b), so it's negative as a signed 16-bit value. Sign extension fills the upper 16 bits with 1s: 0xffffbabe.

questions.q: Why does the compiler sign-extend `a` before storing it into `b[1]`?
choices: a is a signed short being assigned to a signed int, so widening it must keep its (possibly negative) value
Stack slots must always hold sign-extended values
movswl is faster than a plain mov
The red zone requires 32-bit aligned values
questions.explain: Converting a signed 16-bit value to a signed 32-bit int must preserve its value, which means copying the sign bit into the new upper bits. That's what sign extension does.

questions.q: b is an `int b[6]` and analysis shows b[1] is at -0x2c(%rbp). Where is b[4]?
choices: -0x1c(%rbp)
questions.explain: Array elements are at increasing addresses, 4 bytes apart for int. b[4] = b[1] + 3*4 = -0x2c + 0xc = -0x20. (b[2] = -0x28, b[3] = -0x24, b[5] = -0x1c.)

questions.q: The lowest stack access in ArrayLocalVariable is -0x2c(%rbp). How many gdb 'words' (the w size) must you display, starting at rbp-0x2c, to cover everything up to rbp?
questions.explain: 0x2c = 44 bytes, and a gdb word is 4 bytes, so 44 / 4 = 11 words (for example, display/11wx $rbp-0x2c).

questions.q: In gdb's examine/display size letters, how big are a 'w' (word) and an 'h' (halfword)?
choices: w = 2 bytes, h = 1 byte
w = 4 bytes, h = 2 bytes
w = 8 bytes, h = 4 bytes
w = 2 bytes, h = 4 bytes
questions.explain: A gdb 'word' is 4 bytes, but in Intel terms a word is 2 bytes. A gdb halfword (h) is 2 bytes, the Intel word size. So `x/1hx $rbp-0x2` shows just the 16-bit 0xbabe.

questions.q: In ArrayLocalVariable, how can you tell which stack offset holds which local variable?
choices: Match the values each instruction writes to the C source: 0xbabe goes to -0x2(%rbp), so that's a; the 64-bit constant goes to -0x10(%rbp), so that's c; the sign-extended a goes to -0x2c(%rbp), so that's b[1]
Locals always appear in declaration order at -0x4, -0x8, -0xc, and so on
The disassembly labels each offset with its variable name
Larger variables are always placed closer to rbp
questions.explain: Unoptimized code stores each value right after computing it, so you can tie each offset to a variable by matching the constants and operations to the C statements.

questions.q: To compute `b[4] = b[1] + c` (c is a long long), the code loads c into rax but then does a 32-bit `add %edx,%eax` and stores eax into b[4]. Why is a 32-bit add enough?
choices: b[4] is an int, so only the low 32 bits of the sum are kept, and those depend only on the low 32 bits of b[1] and c
long long values are only 32 bits on Linux
The add instruction can't operate on 64-bit registers
The upper half of c is added later by the sign extension
questions.explain: Storing the result into a 4-byte int keeps only its low 32 bits, and the low 32 bits of a sum depend only on the low 32 bits of the operands. So adding edx (b[1]) to eax (the low half of c) gives exactly the value stored into b[4] and returned in eax.
